title: Photoelectrocatalytic-microbial biohybrid for succinic acid synthesis

paper_content.abstract: Succinic acid is an important platform chemical traditionally produced via energy-intensive and environmentally unfriendly processes. Actinobacillus succinogenes offers a sustainable biosynthetic route, yet its productivity is constrained by limited intracellular electron transfer. Here, we develop a photoelectrocatalytic–microbial biohybrid system to overcome these metabolic bottlenecks. Adaptive laboratory evolution using gold nanoparticles establishes an enhanced charge-transfer pathway in Actinobacillus succinogenes, which is subsequently immobilized on a layer-by-layer NiO@PAA@NHS (NiO nanosheets coated with hydrogel of polyacrylic acid (PAA) grafted with N-Hydroxysuccinimide (NHS)) photoelectrode to construct a NiO@PAA@NHS/Au@Actinobacillus succinogenes biohybrid. Under simulated solar illumination at −0.3 V vs. RHE, the system delivers a photocurrent density of 1.9 mA cm-2, a CO2 conversion efficiency of 67%, and a succinic acid production rate of 1.41 ± 0.04 g L-1 h-1 cm-2. This work demonstrates an effective strategy for coupling solar energy with microbial metabolism for scalable, carbon-neutral chemical production.
paper_content.introduction:
Succinic acid, alternatively referred to as amber acid or 1,4-butanedioic acid, is a promising raw material to produce 1,4-butanediol, γ-butyrolactone, tetrahydrofuran, 2-pyrrolidinone, and polybutylene succinate1,2. This versatile compound is widely applied across industries, including chemical synthesis, food flavoring and preservation, pharmaceutical manufacturing, and the development of biodegradable plastics3,4. Therefore, it is listed as one of the twelve high-value chemicals by the U.S. Department of Energy5. The market for succinic acid is anticipated to experience a compound annual growth rate of 10.6%, and it is projected that by the year 2026, the market will surpass the value of 200 million US dollars6. Currently, most of commercially available succinic acid is produced by chemical process, in which liquefied petroleum gas or maleic anhydride is used as a starting material7,8. However, the process poses several environmental and health concerns due to the release of greenhouse gases and pollutants, and the by-products generated in this process are toxic and require careful disposal9. Therefore, there is a growing interest in developing more sustainable and environmentally friendly alternatives to the current chemical production methods of succinic acid.

Recent analysis has shown that bacterial fermentative production of succinic acid from renewable resources can be more cost-effective than the petroleum-based processes10–12. Many different microorganisms have been screened and studied for succinic acid production13–15. Among them, Actinobacillus succinogenes (A. succinogenes), a naturally succinic acid-producing strain isolated from bovine rumen, is one of the most intensively investigated bacterium for succinic acid production16. The A. succinogenes has a natural capacity to convert both pentose and hexose sugars into succinic acid as an intermediate of the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle17. Upon the absorption of the substrate glucose by the bacteria, it is converted into phosphoenolpyruvate (PEP), marking the beginning of the metabolic divergence into two distinct pathways18,19. One pathway is dedicated to the production of the desired product, succinic acid, and is primarily governed by the enzyme phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase (Pepck). Under the catalysis of PEPCK and with the aid of coenzymes such as NADH, CO2 is incorporated into the metabolic pathway. PEP undergoes a series of enzymatic transformations, initially forming oxaloacetate, which is then reduced to malate through the action of malate dehydrogenase, utilizing NADH. Subsequently, malate is converted to fumarate by fumarase, and finally, fumarate is transformed into succinic acid, the target product, in a reaction catalyzed by fumarate reductase. The other metabolic route, dominated by pyruvate kinase (PK), is responsible for the synthesis of by-products such as formic acid, acetic acid, and ethanol. This metabolic flexibility allows the bacteria to adapt to varying environmental conditions and substrate availabilities, optimizing the overall efficiency of succinic acid production within the PEC-bacterial biohybrid system. This metabolic pathway ingeniously incorporates CO2 20–22, rendering it an optimal candidate for transforming lignocellulosic sugars and CO2 into bio-products from sustainable feedstocks, and providing an additional advantage of contributing to the carbon peaking and carbon neutrality goals23–26. However, the inherent metabolic processes of microorganisms in the context of fermentation-based chemical synthesis impose constraints on the potential for increased product yields. Presently, two strategies have been posited to surmount these limitations and to augment production metrics. The first strategy encompasses genetic engineering, leveraging targeted modifications to refine and optimize metabolic routes27,28. However, compared to commonly industrial microorganisms, the repertoire of genetic modification techniques for A. succinogenes is rather confined, which hinders the rate of strain improvement through genetic engineering. The alternative paradigm introduces the assembly of biohybrids, which entails the amalgamation of nanomaterials with bacterial systems to supply the microorganisms with surplus electrons and energy, consequently elevating production levels29–31. Consequently, in response to the growing demand for sustainable and environmentally friendly production methods, the engineering of biohybrids emerges as an innovative and exceptionally prospective pathway for enhancing succinic acid yields. While this approach needs to address the critical requirements for sustainable energy input, efficient charge transfer, and intracellular electron transport, which are essential for enhancing succinic acid yields.

The photoelectrocatalytic-bacterial (PEC-bacterial) biohybrid system is a good candidate to harness sustainable solar energy and to drive the production of succinic acid from CO2 and renewable resources. This system integrates a photoelectrode with A. succinogenes, where the photoelectrode generates electrons upon illumination, and these electrons are transferred to the bacteria, facilitating the assimilation of CO2 into succinic acid. As the most active bacteria at the biotic-abiotic interface are those directly connected to the photoelectrode, and close microbial-electrode interactions can promote electron transport and CO2 reduction efficiency32,33. Therefore, the effective integration of the photoelectrode with the bacteria is the prerequisites for efficient charge transfer in the PEC-bacterial system. We draw inspiration from several innovative studies, for example, Zhang34 has designed 3D printed hierarchical column array electrodes that significantly boost bacterial loading efficiency. Additionally, Erwin Reisner35 has proposed an IO-ITO electrode with a hydrophilic surface and porous structure, which facilitates bacterial affinity. Liu36 has also contributed to the field with an in-situ chemical reaction-mediated covalent localization strategy of bacteria, where thiolated bacteria bind to poly(disulfide)s-abundant mucin located at various tissue interfaces.

Herein, the photoelectrode is designed with a typical p-type semiconductor of NiO nanosheets, which is coated with hydrogel of poly acrylic acid (PAA) grafted with N-Hydroxysuccinimide (NHS) (NiO@PAA@NHS). Hydrogel is a highly water-containing, three-dimensional network-structured material with excellent biocompatibility and ability to load a range of biologically active substances, such as bacteria, which not only have good adhesion to the bacteria, but also promote bacterial colonization and activity over a long period of time37,38. Furthermore, to ensure efficient extracellular and intracellular electron transport, the gold nanoparticles (Au NPs) are incubated into bacteria through an adaptive laboratory evolution (ALE) strategy, pioneered by Prof. Peidong Yang39, to form a conductive bridge that allows electrons generated extracellularly to be transported across the bacterial membrane and into the metabolic pathways of the bacteria. Moreover, the Au-ALE process can optimize the bacteria’s electroactivity, enhancing their ability to acquire and transfer electrons, which in turn improves interfacial charge transport while maintaining bacterial vitality40. Therefore, the PEC-bacterial biohybrid of NiO@PAA@NHS/Au@A. succinogenes provides necessary metabolic energy to boost succinic acid production, and reach a high succinic acid yield rate of 1.41 ± 0.04 g L−1 h−1 cm−2 (0.012 ± 0.0003 mol mol L−1 h−1 cm−2) at one atmospheric pressure saturated with CO2 under illumination of solar light. This PEC-bacterial biohybrid is expected to be applied in large-scale, low-cost succinic acid production, providing another direction for CO2 reduction, and sustainably producing high-value long-chain hydrocarbons. This innovative approach leverages solar energy and biohybrid technology to produce high-value chemicals in a sustainable and environmentally friendly manner.
paper_content.results:
Construction of the PEC-Bacterial Biohybrid System
The PEC-bacterial biohybrid reactor, as schematically illustrated in Fig. 1a, is designed with a NiO@PAA@NHS/Au@A. succinogenes biohybrid photoelectrode to leverage the metabolic capabilities of A. succinogenes for the synthesis of succinic acid from CO2 under solar light illumination. Figure 1b illustrates the interaction between the PAA@NHS hydrogel and the A. succinogenes cell membrane. The ester groups (C=O) on the hydrogel surface interact with the amino groups (N-H) of membrane proteins through possible amide linkage formation, promoting robust bacterial adhesion on the photoelectrode surface. However, the current spectroscopic evidence only indicates interfacial coupling rather than definitive covalent bond formation. Notably, these bacteria have been adapted after Au-adaptive laboratory evolution (ALE) process, introducing Au NPs near the inner cell membrane. This strategic introduction of Au NPs establishes an efficient charge transfer pathway, enhancing the charge transfer efficiency and, consequently, increasing the yield of PEC production of succinic acid. This innovative approach highlights the potential of combining biocompatible materials with nanoscale engineering to optimize bio-photoelectrochemical systems.

Characterization of bacterial modification and surface immobilization
The Au NPs were introduced into A. succinogenes with an ALE strategy. As illustrated in Fig. 2a, this strategy enabled the bacteria to adapt to and tolerate the presence of these Au NPs. This process is essential for creating a biohybrid system where the bacteria can utilize the Au NPs for enhanced electron transfer. In the ALE process, A. succinogenes were initially exposed to a low concentration of Au ions, allowing the bacteria to encounter the Au ions without causing immediate toxicity. The Au ions were taken up by the bacteria, possibly through active transport mechanisms or simple diffusion41. Once inside the cells, the Au ions are reduced to Au NPs by reductive substances present in the bacterial cells, such as NADH or other biomolecules with reducing properties42–44. As the bacteria are exposed to increasing concentrations of Au ions over time, they develop mechanisms to tolerate and manage the presence of these Au NPs. The Au-ALE allows the bacteria not only to tolerate but also to thrive in the presence of Au NPs, thus significantly enhancing their survival rates.

Figure 2b displays a thin-sectioned transition electron microscopy (TEM) image of wild A. succinogenes, where it can be observed that the morphology is intact and spherical. As shown in Fig. 2c, the ALE of A. succinogenes with Au ions has resulted in the bacteria embedding Au NPs within their cellular structure, particularly near the inner wall of the bacterial cell membrane. The size distribution of Au NPs in bacteria is shown in Supplementary Fig. 1, with an average particle size of approximately 38 nm. The high-angle annular dark-field scanning transmission electron microscopy (HAADF-STEM) image in Fig. 2d reveals distinct bright spots, which, according to this characterization method, indicate a higher atomic number of an element. The brightness of the spots corresponds to the presence of elements with higher atomic numbers, and in this case, it further demonstrates the presence of Au NPs within the bacterial cells, located near the inner wall of the cell membrane. The corresponding energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) mapping image in Fig. 2e for Au@A. succinogenes also confirms the successful entry of Au NPs into the bacterial cells. The EDS data show a higher concentration of Au near the cell membrane, suggesting that the Au NPs were not only internalized by the bacteria but also accumulated near the cell membrane, as evidenced by the intense EDS signal for Au in that region. This membrane-associated localization of Au NPs can be attributed to their intracellular formation mechanism. During the ALE process, A. succinogenes gradually adapted to increasing concentrations of HAuCl4, reducing Au3+ to Au0 likely using intracellular reductants such as NADH and NADH-dependent reductases. Since many of these reductases are enriched at or near the inner membrane, the nucleation of Au0 preferentially occurs in that region, resulting in the accumulation of Au NPs adjacent to the membrane. Although Fig. 2e shows the overall Au distribution, this proximity to the membrane is further supported by HAADF-STEM and EDS mapping. Such spatial positioning is essential for the Au NPs to serve as intracellular conduits for electron transfer, bridging the photoelectrode-derived electrons with bacterial metabolic pathways without disrupting cellular viability.

Despite the presence of these Au NPs, we have observed that the bacteria continue to divide (Supplementary Fig. 2). Moreover, the uniform distribution of Au NPs within each bacterium further substantiates the successful complexation of the Au NPs and their excellent biocompatibility. Furthermore, we compared the viability of A. succinogenes cultured directly in a high-concentration Au ion solution (2 μM) versus those cultured using a stepwise acclimation approach (0.5 μM, 1 μM, 1.5 μM, and 2 μM) with flow cytometry (Supplementary Fig. 3). As shown in Fig. 2f, the apoptotic analysis revealed that 73.1% of the 100,000 bacteria treated directly with 2 μM HAuCl4 underwent apoptosis. In contrast, when bacteria were adapted to 2 μM HAuCl4, the survival rates surged to 89.1%. This significant difference demonstrates that the ALE approach is an effective way to introduce high concentrations of Au NPs within bacterial cells, which is crucial for enhancing charge transfer efficiency. All these micromorphological and elemental evidence provide compelling evidence of the intracellular localization of Au NPs, highlighting their potential role in facilitating electron transfer processes within the bacteria and potentially enhancing the overall efficiency of the PEC-bacterial biohybrid system.

The Au-ALE A. succinogenes bacteria are adsorbed onto the surface of photoelectrodes, which are prepared by coating a PAA@NHS hydrogel on NiO nanosheets (Fig. 2g). We performed FTIR spectroscopy to analyze the interfacial chemical environment (Supplementary Fig. 4). The free A. succinogenes spectrum shows distinct amide I (1627 cm−1) and amide II (1533 cm−1) bands45. After immobilization on NiO@PAA@NHS, new features emerge at 1685 cm−1 and 1625 cm−1 with significant attenuation of the amide II signal. This behavior suggests enhanced hydrogen bonding and possible amide-linkage interactions between bacterial surface proteins and the NHS-activated hydrogel layer46. The weakened amide II band is partly due to spectral overlap with the C=O stretching of the hydrogel (≈1710 cm−1) and the broad O-H/N-H bending envelope (1550–1650 cm−1), indicating that these shifts reflect interfacial coupling rather than definitive covalent bond formation. Additionally, the band at 1043 cm−1 is attributed to C–O–C stretching vibrations of polysaccharides present on the bacterial cell wall or C–O stretching in polyacrylic acid (PAA)47. After incubating the bacteria-with NiO@PAA@NHS, NiO@PAA, and bare NiO electrodes in 0.1 M PBS solution for 30 min, CLSM analysis (Supplementary Fig. 5) revealed negligible bacterial detachment from the NiO@PAA@NHS electrode, whereas NiO@PAA and bare NiO controls showed stronger fluorescence signals corresponding to higher bacterial release. It is likely that the NHS-activated hydrogel layer could improve interfacial adhesion and biofilm stability.

The NiO nanosheets, synthesized via a hydrothermal method on nickel foam, exhibit a distinct lamellar structure with a fine, fluffy nanostructure as observed in the SEM image (Supplementary Fig. 6). High-resolution TEM (HR-TEM) analysis reveals an interplanar spacing of 0.23 nm (Supplementary Fig. 7), corresponding to the (200) plane of NiO, confirmed by the XRD pattern (Supplementary Fig. 8).

The formation of the NiO@PAA@NHS sample was characterized using FTIR, Raman spectroscopy, and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS). The FTIR analysis (Supplementary Fig. 9) shows peaks at 1710 cm−1, 1423 cm−1, and 1270 cm−1, corresponding to the stretching vibration of the C=O bond, the scissor bending vibration of -CH2, and the stretching vibration of C-N, respectively48. A new Raman peak (Supplementary Fig. 10) after encapsulating PAA@NHS can be assigned to C-H asymmetric stretching of PAA@NHS. The XPS data indicate a new N1s peak and variation of O1s peaks, evidencing the formation of the NiO@PAA@NHS material (Supplementary Fig. 11). The nanosheet structures are well-preserved after the PAA@NHS hydrogel coating, maintaining a predominantly rounded and smooth morphology (Supplementary Fig. 12). A TEM image further confirms the wrapping of PAA/NHS around the surface of the NiO nanosheets (Supplementary Fig. 13), and the crystal structure of NiO remains unchanged after the PAA@NHS coating, as shown by the XRD pattern (Supplementary Fig. 8). The elemental distribution on NiO@PAA@NHS is revealed by a HAADF-STEM image and corresponding EDS elemental mapping images (Supplementary Fig. 14), showing a uniform distribution of Ni, N, and O elements, with the nitrogen originating from the NHS component within the PAA@NHS hydrogel. Collectively, these results confirm the successful construction of the NiO@PAA@NHS photoelectrode.

After the successful fabrication of the NiO@PAA@NHS electrode, the A. succinogenes after the Au-ALE were adsorbed onto its surface. SEM analysis, as depicted in Fig. 2h, i, conducts a comparative assessment of bacterial cell counts and clearly illustrates a pronounced increase in bacterial colonization on the NiO@PAA@NHS photoelectrode surface. This increase indicates a marked enhancement in bacterial adhesion attributable to the presence of the PAA@NHS hydrogel layer. A quantitative summary of A. succinogenes bacteria is presented in Fig. 2j, showing an average bacterial count of 0.16 × 106/mm2 on pristine NiO. In contrast, this count significantly rose to 2.6 × 106/mm2 on the NiO@PAA@NHS surface. Such a substantial enhancement in bacterial adhesion highlights the critical role of surface functionalization in augmenting bacterial adhesion and metabolic activity within the PEC-bacterial biohybrid system. This surface modification is pivotal for creating a conducive environment for bacterial attachment and activity, thereby enhancing the overall performance of the biohybrid system.

Photoelectrocatalytic performance of the biohybrid system
The PEC activity of NiO@PAA@NHS/Au@A. succinogenes biohybrid was evaluated by linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) in an Ar- or CO2-saturated electrolyte, in the dark or under illumination of simulated solar light (AM1.5G, 100 mW cm−2). As depicted in Fig. 3a, in the Ar-saturated electrolyte, the NiO@PAA@NHS/Au@A. succinogenes biohybrid exhibited a weak photocurrent response. However, in the CO2-saturated electrolyte, the current densities both in dark and under illumination were significantly enhanced, indicating effective CO2 reduction involvement in succinic acid production. The succinic acid yields were compared under CO2 and Ar atmospheres with or without the addition of Mg(OH)2CO3. As a pH neutralizer, the Mg(OH)2CO3 also served as an additional carbon source during the reaction process. Therefore, when Ar was introduced without the addition of basic magnesium carbonate, A. succinogenes essentially produced no succinic acid (Supplementary Fig. 15). Furthermore, the current density on the NiO@PAA@NHS/Au@A. succinogenes biohybrid under illumination was much higher than that in the dark, suggesting more effective CO2 reduction and a higher succinic acid yield in the PEC model than that in the electrocatalytic (EC) model. These observations underscore the system’s capacity for CO2 reduction and its efficient harnessing of photogenerated electrons, thereby enhancing succinic acid production.

The succinic acid yield rate of the NiO@PAA@NHS/Au@A. succinogenes biohybrid was evaluated under various operational models, revealing significant differences in performance. As presented in Fig. 3b, the PEC model (PEC-biohybrid) demonstrated the highest yield rate of 1.41 ± 0.04 g L−1 h−1 cm−2 (0.012 ± 0.0003 mol mol L−1 h−1 cm−2), showcasing its superior efficiency in succinic acid production. This outcome underscores the effectiveness of integrating light-based energy input to enhance bacterial metabolism and succinic acid generation. The EC model (EC-biohybrid) followed with a yield rate of 0.75 ± 0.03 g L−1 h−1 cm−2, while the photocatalytic model (PC-biohybrid) exhibited a rate around 0.58 ± 0.06 g L−1 h−1 cm−2. In contrast, the biohybrid under dark and open circuit conditions had the lowest yield rate of 0.21 ± 0.04 g L−1 h−1 cm−2. These results suggest that external energy input, particularly through the PEC model, can substantially increase the rate of succinic acid production by A. succinogenes, highlighting the potential of this approach in bioprocess optimization and sustainable chemical production.

Figure 3c provides a comparative analysis of the succinic acid yield rate across four biohybrid systems, including NiO@PAA@NHS/Au@A. succinogenes, NiO@PAA/Au@A. succinogenes, NiO/Au@A. succinogenes, and Au@A. succinogenes. The NiO@PAA@NHS/Au@A. succinogenes biohybrid system reaches the highest yield rate. The NiO@PAA/Au@A. succinogenes system also performs well, with a yield rate of 0.98 ± 0.06 g L−1 h−1 cm−1. In contrast, the NiO/Au@A. succinogenes, and the Au@A. succinogenes, which lack the additional components, show lower yield rates of just 0.47 ± 0.03 g L−1 h−1 cm−1 and 0.21 ± 0.02 g L−1 h−1 cm−1, respectively. Furthermore, the CO2 conversion efficiency (Supplementary Fig. 16) and glucose conversion rate (Supplementary Fig. 17) were systematically analyzed across different systems. The NiO@PAA@NHS/Au@A. succinogenes biohybrid system demonstrated superior performance, achieving a remarkable 67% CO2 conversion rate along with a glucose conversion yield of 0.78 g/g glucose. These results underscore the importance of the biohybrid composition in maximizing succinic acid yield, with the NiO@PAA@NHS/Au@A. succinogenes system demonstrating the most promising results due to the contribution of Au NPs acting as an efficient charge transfer bridge and the hydrogel’s effective adhesion to bacteria.

The photocurrent densities at different applied potentials of NiO@PAA@NHS/Au@A. succinogenes biohybrid was compared and is presented in Fig. 3d. The biohybrid shows stable photocurrent performance, and the photocurrent density increases with more negative potentials, indicating efficient charge separation and transport at the PEC-bacterial model. In order to further screen the appropriate potential for succinic acid production, we comprehensively compared the succinic acid yield rate at different potentials. As shown in Fig. 3e, the NiO@PAA@NHS/Au@A. succinogenes biohybrid system reaches the highest succinic acid yield rate at −0.3 V (vs RHE), which can be attributed to a balance between electron supply and the metabolic demands of the bacteria. At −0.2 V (vs RHE), the photocurrent density is lower, suggesting that the electrons supply to the biohybrid system is insufficient to meet the bacteria’s needs for succinic acid production (Supplementary Fig. 18). This could be due to less efficient charge separation or a lower driving force for electron transfer at this potential. With increasingly negative potentials (−0.2 to −0.5 V vs RHE), the photocurrent density and H2 evolution on the bare NiO@PAA@NHS photocathode both rose markedly (Supplementary Fig. 19). However, the highest succinic acid yield occurred at −0.3 V, indicating that excessive bias promotes H2 generation rather than electron transfer to the bacteria for CO2 fixation49. These results suggest that hydrogen evolution and transmembrane electron uptake are competitive processes, and that −0.3 V represents an optimal potential where interfacial charge transfer and microbial metabolism are effectively balanced.

In addition to succinic acid, other byproducts such as acetic acid, formic acid, and pyruvic acid were also measured in the biohybrid system. As presented in Fig. 3f, the yield rate of succinic acid is the fastest, indicating that it is the predominant product under the given conditions, and it accounts for 57.18% of the total yield. To further analyze possible gaseous products, gas chromatography (GC) was performed to quantify H2 and CO generated during the reaction. As shown in Supplementary Fig. 20, trace amounts of CO (~425.7 nmol after 3 h) and small amounts of H2 (~144 μmol after 8 h) were detected. The calculated Faradaic efficiencies were 48.3% for the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) and only 0.38% for CO formation from CO2 reduction, confirming that gaseous CO2RR products are negligible and that the majority of photogenerated electrons are utilized for microbial succinate synthesis rather than abiotic gas formation.

The long-term stability of the PEC-biohybrid system for succinic acid generation was evaluated to monitor the photocurrent (Supplementary Fig. 18) and cyclic PEC reactions (Supplementary Fig. 21). The photocurrent changes were negligible when the biohybrid system was operated at −0.3 V vs RHE over a period of 10 h, indicating a stable transfer of photoelectrons from the electrode to the bacteria. In addition, succinic acid yield was assessed over five consecutive cyclic reactions. There is a gradual decrease in succinic acid production after 5 days, which can be attributed to minor degradation of both the electrode materials and bacterial viability under prolonged PEC conditions.

Maintaining a consistent output is essential for the viability and efficiency of industrial production processes. Therefore, the continuous production of succinic acid by a biohybrid system under conditions that simulate day and night cycles, alternating between PEC and EC modes, was investigated. As shown in Fig. 3g, the simulation of a light–dark cycle of 12 h effectively mirrors the biohybrid system’s capability to produce succinic acid for 5 days, highlighting the system’s potential for sustained industrial application. It should be noted that the “superior efficiency” claim refers specifically to the higher succinic acid productivity achieved under PEC conditions (during the light phase), whereas EC conditions alone exhibit a relatively lower production rate. Nevertheless, alternating between PEC and EC modes is crucial to maintaining continuous and stable succinic acid production over extended periods.

Furthermore, to evaluate the biocompatibility of the biohybrid system, confocal laser scanning microscope (CLSM) images were taken before and after the PEC reaction (Supplementary Fig. 22). A. succinogenes was stained with the BB cell Probe N01™/PI fluorescent probe. The BB cell Probe N01™ can emit bright green fluorescence upon excitation due to its ability to penetrate the cell membrane of living bacteria. In contrast, PI can only stain dead bacteria, showing red fluorescence after excitation50–53. Compared to A. succinogenes before the reaction, after an extended reaction period, there was a significant increase in green fluorescence intensity and a slight enhancement in the red fluorescence signal. This suggests that the bacteria were able to rapidly multiply within the system and that there was a natural generational turnover occurring. Additionally, a colony-forming unit (CFU) assay was conducted to assess bacterial viability (Supplementary Fig. 23). There was an increase in the bacterial count after the long-term reaction. Collectively, these findings further suggest that the A. succinogenes in the biohybrid system possesses robust self-repairing and self-replicating capabilities, indicating that the bacteria remain viable and active before and after the reaction, which is crucial for sustained functionality in industrial applications.

The succinic acid yield rates in a PEC-biohybrid system were compared with various other biohybrid systems and bacterial strains under different reaction conditions (Supplementary Table 1). As shown in Fig. 3h, the biohybrid system operating in PEC mode demonstrated the highest succinic acid production rate among the systems tested, which is a testament to its superior efficiency. The PEC-biohybrid system’s superior succinic acid yield rate, high biocompatibility, and long-term stability position it as a leading candidate for industrial-scale production and commercialization of this essential chemical.

During succinic acid biosynthesis, synergistic catalysis between glucose and CO2 is essential. The carbon origin distribution in succinate was precisely mapped through comprehensive 1H and 13C nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopic analysis. In the 1H NMR spectrum (Supplementary Fig. 24a), the methylene proton peak appears at 2.34 ppm. Following 13CO2 labeling, this signal remains unchanged. However, when labeled with 13C6H12O6, the peak splits into a doublet, demonstrating that 13C from glucose is incorporated into the succinic acid carbon skeleton through metabolic processes, inducing complex coupling (13C-13C coupling). For the 13C-NMR analysis (Supplementary Fig. 24b), the carboxyl carbon (-COOH) resonates at 181 ppm, and its signal intensity increases significantly after 13CO2 labeling, confirming that CO2 fixation directly contributes to the carboxyl carbon. And the methylene carbon (-CH2-) appears at 32 ppm, and both the methylene and carboxyl carbon signals show notable enhancement upon 13C6H12O6 labeling. This indicates that the glucose carbon skeleton, via glycolysis/TCA cycle metabolism, generates the methylene group and partially contributes to the carboxyl carbons of succinic acid. This dual-labeling NMR analysis provides clear evidence for the distinct biosynthetic origins of succinic acid’s carbon backbone.

Mechanistic insights into enhanced succinic acid production
Figure 4a presents a schematic overview of succinic acid biosynthesis in the NiO@PAA@NHS/Au@A. succinogenes biohybrid, emphasizing glucose assimilation and redox modulation along the C4 metabolic pathway under photoelectrocatalytic conditions. In this system, electronic interactions at the biohybrid interface modulate intracellular redox states, thereby favoring succinate formation. Based on the additional electrochemical and control experiments, we suggest that direct electron transfer (DET) across the Au-mediated electrode-bacteria interface serves as the primary pathway, whereas H2-mediated electron transfer makes a minor contribution under conditions study. Cyclic voltammetry (CV) analysis (Supplementary Fig. 25a) revealed that wild-type A. succinogenes exhibited intrinsically weak electroactivity, while Au-adapted cells showed pronounced redox peaks centered at approximately +0.15 V (vs RHE). The current density nearly doubled from ~0.45 mA cm−2 to ~0.85 mA cm−2. In contrast, the CV profile of the cell-free supernatant was mostly featureless, ruling out contributions from soluble mediators or residual Au ions (Supplementary Fig. 25b). These results suggest that the Au nanoparticles formed near the inner membrane act as conductive nanoscale bridges, facilitating charge exchange between the photoelectrode and bacterial metabolic pathways without disrupting cellular viability. Despite the presence of these Au NPs, we have observed that the bacteria continue to divide (Supplementary Fig. 2). Moreover, the uniform distribution of Au NPs within each bacterium further substantiates the successful complexation of the Au NPs and their excellent biocompatibility. Furthermore, we compared the viability of A. succinogenes cultured directly in a high-concentration Au ion solution (2 μM) versus those cultured using a stepwise acclimation approach (0.5 μM, 1 μM, 1.5 μM, and 2 μM) with flow cytometry (Supplementary Fig. 3). As shown in Fig. 2f, the apoptotic analysis revealed that 73.1% of the 100,000 bacteria treated directly with 2 μM HAuCl4 underwent apoptosis. In contrast, when bacteria were adapted to 2 μM HAuCl4, the survival rates surged to 89.1%. This significant difference demonstrates that the ALE approach is an effective way to introduce high concentrations of Au NPs within bacterial cells, which is crucial for enhancing charge transfer efficiency. All these micromorphological and elemental evidence provide compelling evidence of the intracellular localization of Au NPs, highlighting their potential role in facilitating electron transfer processes within the bacteria and potentially enhancing the overall efficiency of the PEC-bacterial biohybrid system. The precise route of electron transport across the bacterial membrane, however, requires further elucidation. Although a minor indirect pathway may coexist, its contribution is small. Umol amounts of H2 generated at the photocathode surface can be oxidized by membrane-bound hydrogenases and introduced into the bacterial redox network; however, the addition of external H2 caused only a marginal increase in succinic acid production (Supplementary Fig. 26), confirming that the H2-mediated route contributes minimally compared with the dominant DET process.

Fluorescence lifetime measurements (Fig. 4b) showed that Au@A. succinogenes exhibited a lifetime of 1.89 ns, representing a 45% reduction relative to the control, demonstrating that the incorporation of Au nanoparticles substantially accelerates intracellular electron transfer and charge separation.

To gain a deeper understanding of the internal metabolism of A. succinogenes, the relative ATP level and NADH/NAD+ ratios were compared among three groups: A. succinogenes, NiO@PAA@NHS/A. succinogenes, and NiO@PAA@NHS/Au@A. succinogenes. As depicted in Fig. 4c, the ATP content in A. succinogenes increased by 21% upon biofilm formation with NiO@PAA@NHS, and this increase was even more pronounced, reaching 107%, in the NiO@PAA@NHS/Au@A. succinogenes system. This substantial boost in ATP is crucial for enhancing biochemical synthesis processes. Additionally, the NADH/NAD+ ratio showed a 32% increase in the NiO@PAA@NHS/A. succinogenes group relative to the pristine A. succinogenes, whereas it exhibited a 78% decrease in the NiO@PAA@NHS/Au@A. succinogenes group, as shown in Fig. 4d. This observed change is largely due to the conversion of NADH to NAD+ during the metabolic pathways leading to succinic acid production. Key enzymes in these pathways, including malate dehydrogenase (MDH), fumarase (FUM), and fumarate reductase (FRD), are involved in the oxidation of NADH to NAD+. Therefore, to direct the bacterial metabolism towards the C4 pathway for succinic acid synthesis, an increased production of NAD+ is necessary, which is facilitated by the PEC process.

To further unravel the mechanisms underlying succinic acid production in different systems, we analyzed the expression levels of key genes associated with mixed-acid synthesis using real-time quantitative reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) (Fig. 4e). Overall, upon attachment to the electrode, the expression of all genes in A. succinogenes was upregulated, indicating that efficient electron supply at the electrode modulates an increase in various metabolic gene products. This upregulation was observed in both the NiO@PAA@NHS/A. succinogenes and NiO@PAA@NHS/Au@A. succinogenes systems. PEPCK and PK are determinants of the C4 and C3 pathways, respectively, while FRD, PflB, and ACK correspond to the production of succinic acid, formic acid, and acetic acid, respectively. Despite the significant upregulation of PK, which is associated with pyruvate kinase, the concentration of pyruvate remained low (Supplementary Fig. 27a). Meanwhile, the product distribution analysis revealed a notable shift in metabolic selectivity upon system modification. For A. succinogenes, succinic acid accounted for merely 44% of total products, while integration of the electrode assembly elevated this proportion to 52% (Supplementary Fig. 27b). These findings indicate that the Au NPs coupled with the photoelectrode not only enhanced the succinic acid production kinetics but also improved its metabolic selectivity. Although the concentrations of acetic and formic acids increased, succinic acid remained the predominant product. This suggests that pyruvate in the system is primarily converted into oxaloacetate and then funneled through the C4 pathway to produce succinic acid.
paper_content.methods:
Strain and media
Actinobacillus succinogenes 130Z (ATCC 55618) was obtained from Professor Wenming Zhang (Nanjing Tech University). The culture medium contained: 5 g/L yeast extract, 9.6 g/L NaH2PO4·2H2O, 15.5 g/L K2HPO4·3H2O, 10 g/L NaHCO3, 30 g/L glucose, 1 g/L NaCl, and 2.5 g/L corn steep liquor at 37°C and 170 rpm. The fermentation medium consisted of 10 g/L yeast extract, 1.36 g/L NaAc, 0.3 g/L Na2HPO4·12H2O, 1.6 g/L NaH2PO4·2H2O, 3 g/L K2HPO4, 1 g/L NaCl, 0.2 g/L MgCl2·6H2O, 7.5 g/L corn steep liquor, 0.2 g/L CaCl2 and 15 g/L Mg(OH)2CO3 for PH neutralizer. Glucose was added after sterilization at a concentration of 30 g/L for fermentation.

Preparation of NiO photocathode
NiO photocathodes were synthesized using a hydrothermal method. Firstly, nickel foam (Ni Foam) was cut into electrode sheets of 1 × 5 cm size, and sequentially cleaned with acetone, alcohol, and distilled water by ultrasonic cleaning for 15 min. The whole NF was directly immersed into a 3 M HCl aqueous solution at 90°C for 20 min in a static immersion to remove surface oxides. The NF was washed with distilled water, and the washed NF was dried under nitrogen. Next, Ni(NO3)2·6H2O (1 mmol) and urea (2 mmol) were dissolved in distilled water (15 mL) and stirred to form a green transparent solution. The pretreated NF (1 cm × 5 cm) was immersed into the solution in a Teflon reactor (25 mL) and kept at 100°C for 12 h. The electrodes were then removed, and the electrodes were placed in a water bath. After removing the electrodes, they were ultrasonically cleaned in ethanol and distilled water. Finally, the electrodes were calcined in a muffle furnace under air atmosphere at 250°C for 3 h.

Preparation of NiO@PAA@NHS photocathode
First, the NiONSs electrodes were immersed in an aqueous acrylic acid solution (30% w/w acrylic acid, 0.03% w/w N,N’-bis(acryloyloxy) cysteamine, and 0.15% w/w 2,2’-azobis(2-methylpropionamidine) dihydrochloride) for 2 h. Then, the immersed hydrogel was sealed and heated at 70°C for 30 min to form the PAA network, and finally dried under nitrogen flow. Subsequently, the prepared NiO@PAANSs electrode was placed in a mixture of 1-ethyl-3-(-3-dimethylaminopropyl) carbodiimide (0.5% w/w) and N-hydroxylthiosuccinimide (0.25% w/w) aqueous solution and soaked for 5 min at room temperature, and then the hydrogel was further dried to obtain the NiO@PAA@NHS NSs photocathode.

Au-ALE of actinobacillus succinogenes
HAuCl4 solution was first added to 20 mL of culture solution to reach a concentration of 0.5 μM. After 12 h of incubation, the bacteria were inoculated into a new 20 mL culture solution, and HAuCl4 solution was added to make the concentration of HAuCl4 of 1.0 μM, 1.5 μM, and 2.0 μM to complete the ALE process. Bacterial cultivation was conducted for 12 h under each HClO4 concentration.

Construction of NiO@PAA@NHS/Au@A. succinogenes biohybrid
Different Au-ALE concentrations of Au@A. succinogenes were inoculated in 20 mL of culture broth, and HAuCl4 solution was added to make the concentrations 1 μM, 2 μM, 3 μM, and 4 μM, respectively. The bacteria were incubated anaerobically in a shaker at 37°C for 12 h. Subsequently, 10,000 g centrifugation was performed to collect the Au@A. succinogenes, and the culture broth was washed with 0.1 M phosphate buffered saline (PBS), washed three times to remove the medium, which was dispersed again in the fermentation broth, and the prepared NiO@PAA@NHS photocathode was placed in solution and incubated for 2 h to construct the NiO@PAA@NHS/Au@A. succinogenes hybrid photoelectrode.

Bacteria density on photoelectrode
High-resolution SEM images were acquired from five randomly selected fields of view on each electrode surface. The images were analyzed using ImageJ software, where bacterial cells were identified through threshold segmentation, followed by manual correction to ensure accuracy. The actual surface area of each field was calculated based on the scale bar, and bacterial counts were normalized accordingly to yield cells per mm2. The reported data represent the mean ± standard deviation of five independent regions.

Photoelectrochemical measurements
The photocatalytic test was completed with a three-electrode system; the reference electrode (RE) was Ag/AgCl, the counter electrode (CE) was a platinum electrode, and the working electrode (WE) was a biohybrid photoelectrode prepared as described in Construction of NiO@PAA@NHS/Au@A. succinogenes biohybrid, and the electrolyte was a bacterial fermentation broth. The reaction was carried out in a 100 mL reactor with a 50 mL working volume. The potential of the saturated Ag/AgCl was converted to that of the reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE) as follows in all the experiments:

ERHE (V) = EAg/AgCl + 0.059 × pH + 0.1976 (1)

CO2 was passed 30 min before the start of the reaction to remove dissolved oxygen. LSV and I–t curve are performed on an Autolab PGATAT302N (Metrohm, Switzerland) electrochemical workstation. For H2 supplementation controls, H2 gas was continuously supplied at 400 mL h−1 during operation. The PEC-biohybrid experiments were performed at an applied potential of −0.3 V versus RHE under illumination, whereas the biohybrid controls were operated in the dark under open-circuit conditions. All other experimental conditions were kept identical to those without external H2. Succinic acid production was quantified by HPLC.

Preparation of the thin-sectioned samples of the hybrid system
The cultured samples were harvested by centrifugation at 10,000 rpm for 10 min and washed three times with 0.1 M phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) to remove culture solution before further characterization. For sample preparation, the hybrid system was dissolved in 1 mL of PBS solution and then fixed using 4% glutaraldehyde at 4°C. After 2 h of fixation, the sample was washed twice with PBS solution at room temperature, then stained with fresh 1% OsO4 in PBS for 1 h. After washing two times with PBS, the sample was sequentially dehydrated in 50%, 70%, 85%, 95% (two times), and 100% (three times) acetone, each time lasting for 10–15 min. Part of the dehydrated sample was embedded and sequentially infiltrated with 1:2, 1:1, and 3:1 resin:acetone, followed by pure resin for three times. The sample was further baked at 70°C for 12 h for complete curing and cut into 70 nm thin sections with a diamond knife. Finally, the sample was deposited onto a Formvar coated copper grid and microscope slide for transmission electron microscopy and confocal fluorescent observation, respectively.

Biohybrid photoelectrode characterizations
Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) images were viewed with a Hitachi-S4800 scanning electron microscope. Transmission electron Microscope (TEM) images were viewed with a JEOL JEM-2100 scanning electron microscope. UV–vis absorption spectrum was recorded on an Evolution 789S spectrophotometer (Shanghai Light Technology Company). Confocal laser scanning microscopy (CLSM) images were obtained by a confocal laser scanning microscope (TCSSP8 MPS MD, LEICA, Germany). The light source was derived from a Xenon lamp (PLS-SXE300, Perfect Light, Beijing) with a filter (AM 1.5G, Perfect Light, Beijing).

Analytical methods
The concentrations of organic acids were determined using Shimadzu high-performance liquid chromatography (Japan). Separation of the samples was achieved using an Ion exclusion chromatography column (Shim-pack SCR-101H) under the following conditions: a column temperature of 55°C, a mobile phase of 100% 0.25 g/L H2SO4, and a flow rate of 0.5 mL/min. Succinic acid, pyruvic acid, formic acid, and acetic acid were detected were detected at 214 nm using an SPD-20A detector. An automatic sampler was used to inject 20 μL of the samples into the chromatograph.

Determination of CO2 conversion efficiency
CO2 flow rate was monitored continuously with a calibrated mass-flow meter and fixed at 7 mL min−1 (at 298 K and 1 atm). The molar CO2 feed rate was therefore:

n(CO2, input) = 7 mL min−1 / 24450 mL mol−1 × t (min) = 2.86 × 10−4 t mol (2)

Succinic acid was detected by HPLC; its molar yield was quantified at different reaction durations. The CO2 conversion efficiency was then calculated as:

CO2 Conversion Rate (%) = (Succinic Acid Yield (mol) / CO2 Input (mol)) × 100% (3)

Glucose concentration analysis
The glucose level was measured using the Beyotime Glucose Assay Kit with O-toluidine, which is based on the chromogenic reaction between glucose and o-toluidine, with quantification performed by colorimetric analysis.

Faradaic efficiency calculation
The Faradaic efficiencies (FEs) for gaseous products were calculated based on the total charge passed during PEC and the quantified number of products formed. The total charge Q (C) was obtained by integrating the photocurrent over the reaction time, and the molar amount of each product n (mol) was determined from gas chromatography (GC) or high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) analysis. The FE for each product was calculated using the following equation:

FE = (n × z × F) / Q × 100% (4)

Where n is the number of moles of the detected product, z is the number of electrons transferred per molecule (2 for both H2 and CO), and F is the Faraday constant (96485 C mol−1).

Cyclic voltammetry measurements
Cyclic voltammetry (CV) was performed in a three-electrode configuration using carbon paper (1 × 1 cm2) as the working electrode, a Pt foil/wire as the counter electrode, and a saturated Ag/AgCl electrode as the reference electrode. The electrolyte was 10 mM phosphate-buffered saline (PBS, pH 7), deaerated with CO2 for 30 min prior to measurements and maintained under a continuous CO2 atmosphere. All measurements were conducted at 37°C. Wild-type and Au@A. succinogenes cells were harvested by centrifugation, washed three times with PBS, and resuspended to OD600 ≈ 2.0. The carbon paper was immersed in the bacterial suspension and incubated anaerobically at 37°C for 4 h to allow cell attachment, then gently rinsed with PBS and used immediately. CV was recorded in the potential range of −0.4 V to 1.4 V (vs RHE) at scan rates of 5–50 mV s−1. Each voltammogram represents a stable response after three consecutive scans. Measurements were repeated with independently prepared bacterial suspensions (n=3). Cell-free supernatants were tested under identical conditions as controls.

NAD+/NADH assay kit measurements
NAD+/NADH assay kit (Beyotime Biotechnology) with WST-8 was used to determine the concentration of NADH and NAD+ in A. succinogenes following the standard manual of the assay kit. All experiments were conducted in the same fermentation broth under identical anaerobic conditions; control and biohybrid samples were cultured for the same duration, with the latter operated under light illumination and applied potential.

Measurement of ATP content
First, 200 μL lysate was gently added to promote cell lysis, and centrifugation was performed to obtain the solution. The solution was added to the 96-well plate, and placed at room temperature for 3 min. After adding 100 μL sample, the RLU value was determined by luminometer.

A. succinogenes viability
During the long-term test, the viability of A. succinogenes has been determined by colony-forming units (CFU) assays. At fixed time intervals, aliquots of 500 μL reaction solution were collected by a sealing syringe. 100 μL of the collected sample was serially diluted with saline. 100 μL of the original and diluted samples were spread on sterilized nutrient agar plates, then incubated at 37°C for 12 h. Finally, the survival number of cells (in CFU) was quantified by counting the visible colonies and the survival rate was calculated.

Staining analysis of bacteria
The bacteria before and after reactions were resuspended in 100 μL BB cell Probe N01 Dye solution A and PI Dye solution B. After incubating at room temperature for 15 min, the bacteria were washed with 0.85% NaCl solution once and then suspended again. Finally, add 20 μL bacterial to the confocal surface dish, and the samples were imaged with CLSM under the excited laser of 488 nm, the emission wavelength of 525 and 620 nm, respectively.

Flow cytometry analysis
A. succinogenes cells were harvested, washed, and resuspended in phosphate-buffered saline (PBS, pH 7.4) prior to measurement. All samples were analyzed using a CytoFLEX flow cytometer (Beckman Coulter, Inc., Brea, CA, USA) equipped with 488 nm and 638 nm lasers. Forward scatter (FSC) and side scatter (SSC) were used to gate bacterial populations based on size and granularity, and a threshold was set on SSC to exclude debris and electronic noise. A minimum of 50,000 events per sample were recorded within the bacterial gate. Data acquisition was performed using CytExpert software (version 2.4, Beckman Coulter), and all collected flow cytometry standard (FCS) files were subsequently analyzed with FlowJo software (version 10.8, BD Biosciences, San Jose, CA, USA). The analysis included gating on singlets, exclusion of outliers, and quantification of fluorescence-positive subpopulations based on unstained and single-stained controls. All experiments were performed in at least three independent biological replicates, and representative histograms or dot plots are shown.

Quantitative RT-PCR
Total RNA Extractor (Trizol) was used to extract total RNA. Real-time quantitative PCR technology refers to the experimental method of quantitative analysis of the starting template by adding a fluorescent group (SYBR green I) to the PCR reaction system, and using the accumulation of fluorescent signals to monitor the PCR process in real time. The 16S rRNA gene was used to standardize the mRNA levels. Primer sequences for qRT-PCR are indicated in Supplementary Table 3. The mRNA level of the target genes was calculated via the 2−ΔΔCT method.

Statistics
Statistical analysis was performed using GraphPad Prism 8.0.2 software using a two-tailed t-test analysis of variance hypothesis. Significant differences are marked as *P < 0.05, **P < 0.01, and ***P < 0.001. All data are presented as mean ± SD. The number of biologically independent samples for each panel was three unless otherwise stated in the figure legends.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
Authors constructed a PEC-bacterial biohybrid system to produce succinic acid in a sustainable method compared to the current. They obtained a very high yield rate and other important conclusions. Before its publication, the following questions should be addressed.
1. In Fig.1, bacteria were adsorbed onto the photoelectrode surface. Have bacteria desorbed from the surface?
2. In Fig.2c,I just noticed black particles located inside bacteria not outside bacteria. Thus did that (no particles outside bacteria) affect electrons transfer from outside to inside?
3. In the manuscript, authors stated "the Au ions are reduced to Au NPs by reductive substances present in the bacterial cells, such as NADH or other biomolecules with reducing properties ". I just wonder what kind of enzymes were responsible for this reduction?
4. There were a lot of by products,leading to a relatively low selectivity of succinic acid (<60%) how to handle them? Did authors make a discussion on this phenomenon？
5. Actinobacillus succinogenes may not belong to electroactive microorganism. In Fig.4a, authors provided a mechanism draft and pointed out that "This internal conductive network not only allows for electron transfer through cytochromes Cyt d I and Cyt d II but also plays a role in the synthesis of additional redox couples". Here, I am still wondering how electrons could transfer from electrode into intracellular? Please provide more information for cytochromes Cyt d I and Cyt d II to prove their functions of electrons transfer.
6. In Fig.3g, 48 h seemed to be a little short to support the long term experimental results and the stability of the biohybrid system.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
This work describes the assembly of A. succinogenes onto photoelectrodes containing a hydrogel, where the authors claim that the hydrogel forms covalent bonds with dangling amines in the cell membrane-bound cytochromes. The authors use this photoelectrochemical hybrid system to generate succinic acid using CO₂ and glucose as carbon sources. They assert that their system outperforms other succinic acid-producing biohybrids and propose a tentative mechanism suggesting that extracellular electron transfer plays a critical role. However, they do not provide experimental evidence to support this proposed mechanism.
The data presentation is generally adequate, although in several instances, additional information would enhance clarity and experimental reproducibility, both in the form of plotted data and methodological details. For example, when comparing succinic acid formation rates in photoelectrochemical biohybrids with electrochemical and photochemical biohybrids, no supporting data—such as chronoamperometry, faradaic efficiency, external quantum yield, or details on the methods used for these experiments—is provided. Additionally, in some plots, it is unclear whether the data were obtained from triplicate experiments.
Overall, while the manuscript presents a concept (covalent linkage of bacteria to a (photo)electrode) that is interesting and noteworthy for the field of biohybrids, the described results from this system provide only an incremental advancement compared to the state-of-the-art literature. Although the figures are well presented, the manuscript would greatly benefit from more exhaustive supporting information to substantiate its claims and a more detailed methods section. Furthermore, throughout the manuscript the authors frequently overstate their claims without sufficient supporting evidence, with the conclusions also included. For these reasons, I believe this manuscript does not meet the standards of Nature Communications. A more specialized journal would be a better fit, particularly after addressing the points raised above.
Regardless of this, I have some questions and suggestions for the authors to address, that I hope will help them to improve their manuscript:
• Abstract: If space allows, including more details on system metrics such as photocurrent, faradaic efficiency, applied potential, and CO₂ conversion efficiency to succinate would strengthen the abstract.
• Terminology: The authors use the terms "domestication" and "acclimated" when describing microbial exposure to gold nanoparticles. Are they referring to adaptive laboratory evolution (ALE)? If so, I recommend replacing these terms with "adaptation", "adapted", and "ALE" for consistency with literature. Additionally, relevant references on ALE, such as Peidong Yang’s work on methanol adaptation of S. ovata, should be cited.
• Gold Nanoparticles (AuNP) & Microbial Exposure:
o How long were the cells exposed to the presence of HAuCl₄ during sequential exposure to 1, 1.5, and 2 µM HAuCl₄ solutions?
o What was the size of the synthesized AuNP? Do the authors believe that plasmonic effects could play a role in this Au-containing biohybrid system?
o The authors claim that AuNP accumulate near the cell membrane, but Figure 2e appears to show AuNP accumulation mainly in the cytoplasm rather than at the membrane. Additionally, this figure is difficult to interpret due to its size; scaling it up could improve clarity.
• Hydrogel Layer & Bacterial Attachment:
o What is the porosity of the hydrogel layer? Can bacteria go inside any pores?
o How do the authors confirm that NHS has reacted with the amine groups on the bacterial surface? This would help support their proposed hypothesis and mechanism, later on.
o The authors claim that A. succinogenes contains dangling NH₂ groups in its membrane-bound cytochromes (Cyt d I and d II), allowing covalent attachment to the hydrogel. However, Ref 40 does not provide any information on amines in membrane-bound cytochromes. Could the authors provide supporting data to their claim and cite appropriate literature references?
o The manuscript frequently refers to "bacterial adhesion" and "surface functionalization" as key factors in improving attachment and not covalent linkage. However, Figure 1 depicts the bacteria as covalently linked to the hydrogel, yet no experimental evidence confirms this covalent bonding (bacteria-NH-CO-hydrogel). Unless further characterization proves covalent attachment, I strongly recommend the authors tone down their claims and modify Figure 1 (and any related figures) accordingly.
o Cell Density in Figure 2j: I could not find details in the methods section regarding how the authors quantified the number of cells per mm². This information should be included.
• Photoelectrochemical (PEC) Experiments:
o What are the faradaic efficiency of all products (coming from the (photo)electrodes and bacteria) and CO₂ conversion efficiency to succinate?
o Were there any byproducts, such as H₂ or CO, formed at the photocathodes?
o The authors show that microbes can produce succinate without CO₂. If PBS medium was used as the electrolyte, was glucose also present as a carbon source in the PEC experiments?
o The manuscript should explicitly state the carbon source used when Ar is present, and the methods section should clarify the media and conditions used for PEC experiments.
o The manuscript lacks experimental data and explanations for electrochemical biohybrids (EC) and photochemical biohybrids (PC) (Figure 3b).
o Regarding Figure 3b, the text only mentions the succinate formation rate, but without additional data, it is unclear why the EC-biohybrid system performs worse than the PEC-biohybrid system.
o Biohybrid experiments typically run for dozens of hours or days, yet the PEC chronoamperometry experiments presented here last only 2 hours. How long were the biohybrid experiments run for Figures 3b, 3c, and 3e?
o In Supplementary Figure 14, how long is each cycle? If it is 10 hours per cycle, this should be explicitly stated for clarity.
o Figure 3g and Supplementary Figure 14 lack error bars—were these plots generated from triplicate experiments?
• Electron Transfer Pathway & Proposed Mechanism:
o Figure 4 clearly depicts the metabolic pathway for microbial CO₂ and glucose conversion to succinic acid. However, the extracellular electron transfer pathway remains unclear. No data (e.g., spectroscopy results) support the hypothesized extracellular electron transfer mechanism. One suggestion is to use time-resolved absorption or vibrational spectroscopy to determine whether the AuNP are reduced/oxidized by internal microbial electron transport chains.
o Based on Ref 40, A. succinogenes contains membrane-bound cytochromes and hydrogenases. Given the (photo)currents at -0.3 V vs. RHE, it is likely that the microbes are not able to uptake all charges and use instead in situ-produced H₂ from the (photo)electrodes as an electron donor for succinic acid production. Therefore, a key control experiment to test this point would be using a knockout strain lacking membrane-bound hydrogenases to see whether succinic acid production is affected under the same conditions.
o To confirm that succinic acid is derived from CO₂ (and not solely from glucose), ¹³CO₂ and ¹³C-glucose labelling experiments should be conducted.
• References:
o References 30 and 31 are incorrect—please verify them and check the rest.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
The authors demonstrate a certain range and novelty compared to the current state of the art. However, I must state that the manuscript, in its current form, does not meet the journal's standards. Please see the comments below for the reasons behind this. Nevertheless, I see potential for the manuscript to meet these standards, provided the comments are addressed.
Major points:
The text describes the evaluation of linear sweep voltammetry between Ar- or CO₂-saturated electrolyte under the influence of light or in darkness. Consequently, a “significantly enhanced” current density is reported both in the light and in the dark under a CO₂ atmosphere. However, two points need to be critically examined: Firstly, the difference between the two experiments conducted in darkness is relatively small. Secondly, the results presented appear to be based on a single measurement (n = 1), which does not allow for any statistically reliable conclusion to be drawn about the observed differences. This should be clearly stated in the discussion. Additionally, the statement on succinate yields under CO₂ or Ar conditions is redundant. It is well known that succinate production in A. succinogenes is CO₂-dependent via the reductive branches of the TCA cycle (see work by James B. McKinlay).
In general, the manuscript and the figures lack precise information on the statistics, particularly regarding the sample size. For instance, some diagrams in Fig. 3/4 display a standard deviation, while others do not. There is no explanation for this either in the captions or in the text. It also remains unclear whether the data are technical or biological replicates. Without this information, it is difficult to assess the reliability of the results, which significantly hinders interpretation, especially as the text frequently refers to “significant” changes. This needs to be clarified.
Regarding the results in Fig. 3g, the data shown correspond to a light-dark cycle intended to simulate a day-night rhythm. The simulations indicate low productivity during the night phases. This implies that the improvement in succinate production rates (g/L/h) emphasised in this manuscript actually occurs only during the day phase. Over a multi-day fermentation process, the average productivity would therefore be lower, calling into question the claimed “superior efficiency” of the system. This limitation should be acknowledged in the discussion.
In general, it would be of interest to analyse the results over a complete fermentation run rather than solely the initial hours. In addition to concentration data, the yield in terms of metabolised glucose (g/g) should also be considered. This would indicate whether not only the production rate of succinate (g/L/h) but also the overall yield (g/g) is improved. In other words, it would determine whether more carbon is actually converted into the target product, succinate. This additional consideration would be crucial in fully evaluating the efficiency of the process.
The manuscript lacks a critical discussion of the challenges posed by the use of light in large-scale applications, despite the method being lauded in the abstract. Typical stirred tank reactors for industrial applications would either require integrated light sources or be replaced by alternative, scalable reactor systems capable of supporting both the electrochemical (electrodes) and photochemical components. At present, the scale-up of bioelectrochemical systems remains a significant challenge. Moreover, research on phototrophic organisms, such as cyanobacteria, has demonstrated that incorporating light into biotechnological processes presents considerable obstacles, including limited light penetration in the reactor (restricting reactor diameter), shading issues, and more. These challenges should be addressed in the discussion and conclusion, especially since the system is described as a “leading candidate for large-scale production and commercialisation.”
The section from “Upon the absorption of the substrate glucose by the bacteria, it is converted into phosphoenolpyruvate (PEP), marking the beginning of the metabolic divergence into two distinct pathways.” to the end of the paragraph serves as a general summary of the metabolism of A. succinogenes. This content is more appropriate for the introduction rather than the results or discussion sections. Furthermore, this section lacks references to substantiate the metabolic processes described. Appropriate sources must be included.
Gene expression analysis of key metabolic enzymes shows an upregulation of all studied enzymes compared to the control, including the enzymes PK, ACK, and PfIB, which are involved in by-product reactions. Consequently, it would be important to compare the yields of by-products between the control and the biohybrids. The text merely states: “Although the concentrations of acetic and formic acids increased,” yet concrete data are missing. By what proportion did the by-products increase? Was there a shift in the ratio between by-products and main products? These aspects are not discussed further, despite the upregulation of the relevant enzymes. This section should be expanded upon, and the corresponding data on by-products should be included.
Minor points:
The manuscript lacks headings and subheadings to provide a clearer structure.
The division of individual figures into up to ten sub-figures, each employing very different methods (e.g., diagrams, microscopic images from different microscopes), makes the manuscript difficult to follow and diminishes readability. To enhance clarity, these illustrations should be divided into multiple smaller figures and presented sequentially within the text.

peer_review_rounds.author_response:
Response to the reviewers’ comments for Manuscript (number: NCOMMS- 25-14204-T)
REVIEWER COMMENTS
Reviewer #1 (Remarks to the Author):
Authors constructed a PEC-bacterial biohybrid system to produce succinic acid in a
sustainable method compared to the current. They obtained a very high yield rate and
other important conclusions. Before its publication, the following questions should be
addressed.
Response: We sincerely appreciate the reviewer’s positive assessment of our work and
their constructive feedback. We have carefully addressed all the raised points in our
revisions and provided detailed responses to each comment. We believe these revisions
now align with the reviewer’s rigorous standards and significantly strengthen the
manuscript. Thank you for your valuable guidance throughout this process.
1. In Fig. 1, bacteria were adsorbed onto the photoelectrode surface. Have bacteria
desorbed from the surface?
Response: We really appreciate the reviewer’s valuable comment. To assess the binding
stability of A. succinogenes on the photoelectrode, we conducted confocal laser
scanning microscope (CLSM) imaging of NiO@PAA@NHS/Au@A. succinogenes
photoelectrode after immersion in PBS solution for 30 and 60 minutes in PEC
conditions. The bacteria were stained with N01 fluorescent dye.
Fig. R1-1 CLSM images of A. succinogenes dyed with BBcellProbe N01 after immersing in PBS
solution for (a) 30 min and (b) 60 min.
As shown in Fig. R1-1, the minimal change in fluorescence intensity indicates
negligible bacterial detachment. These findings, along with FTIR evidence of covalent
amide bond formation between NHS groups and bacterial amines (Fig. R1-2), confirm
the robust and stable immobilization essential for long-term PEC performance.
Fig. R1-2 Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR) of NiO@PAA@NHS/A. succinogenes
and A. succinogenes.
2. In Fig. 2c, I just noticed black particles located inside bacteria not outside bacteria.
Thus, did that (no particles outside bacteria) affect electrons transfer from outside to
inside?
Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for this insightful observation. It is indeed
correct that the Au nanoparticles (Au NPs) are primarily localized intracellularly,
especially near the inner membrane, as confirmed by TEM (Fig. 2c), HAADF-STEM
imaging (Fig. 2d), and EDS elemental mapping (Fig. 2e). This spatial distribution is a
result of the adaptive laboratory evolution (ALE) process, where A. succinogenes were
gradually acclimated to increasing concentrations of HAuCl , enabling them to reduce
dependent reductases. This controlled intracellular accumulation is essential to
forming a conductive nanobridge that facilitates internal redox reactions without
compromising cell viability.
Despite the lack of extracellular Au NPs, the electron transfer from the external
photoelectrode to the bacteria is not hindered. On the contrary, our design enables a
synergistic extracellular-intracellular electron transfer pathway: At the interface, the
NiO@PAA@NHS photoelectrode forms amide bonds with the bacterial surface via
NHS ester groups reacting with membrane-exposed amines, as confirmed by FTIR (Fig.
R1-2). This creates a stable and close-contact interface facilitating efficient electron
injection from the photoelectrode. Within the bacteria, the Au NPs near the membrane
act as electron mediators, accepting electrons that traverse the bacterial envelope and
relaying them deeper into intracellular metabolic pathways.
Fig. R1-3 Fluorescence spectra of A. succinogenes before and after PEC reactions (A.
succinogenes@Au in biohybrid was stained by DiOC (3) green membrane potential dyeing probe
2
in advance, λexc = 482 nm).
To further verify the successful transmembrane electron transport, we conducted
fluorescence spectroscopy experiments using DiOC (3) staining. DiOC (3) is a
2 2
membrane-potential-responsive fluorescent probe that binds to bacterial membranes
and emits green fluorescence. When the membrane potential changes due to external
stimuli, the dye molecules undergo self-polymerization, causing the fluorescence to
redshift. As shown in Fig. R1-3, a redshift in fluorescence post-PEC is presented,
indicating electron accumulation across the bacterial membrane.

Response: Thank you very much for this insightful question. The intracellular reduction
of Au3+ to elemental Au0 is indeed a critical step in the formation of biohybrid
nanostructures and is primarily mediated by NADH-dependent reductase enzymes.
Several studies have identified key enzymes involved in such metal ion reductions: (1)
Correa-Llantén et al. demonstrated that the thermophilic bacterium Geobacillus sp.
strain ID17, isolated from Deception Island, Antarctica, can intracellularly reduce Au3+
to elemental gold (Au) using NADH as a cofactor, with the reduction process mediated
by enzymes (Microbial Cell Factories 2013, 12:75); (2) Dhanasekar et al. reports that
the fungus Bipolaris oryzae produces NADPH-dependent reductase in its cell-free
extract, which rapidly reduces Au3+ ions to Au0, resulting in the formation of gold
nanoparticles within 5–10 minutes (ChemistrySelect 2020, 5, 11522– 11529).
Although A. succinogenes has not yet been reported for specific Au-reductase
enzymes, genome annotations (via KEGG and UniProt) reveal the presence of multiple
NAD(P)H-dependent oxidoreductases, including ferredoxin-NADP⁺ reductase and
dihydrolipoamide dehydrogenase, both of which have redox potentials compatible with
Au3+ reduction. As for mechanism of the enzyme, the NADH-dependent reductase
presumably mediates electron transfer from NADH to Au3+, reducing it to metallic gold.
This enzyme may function in coordination with other intracellular enzymes to complete
the reduction process of Au ions.
Furthermore, the intracellular localization of Au NPs near the inner membrane
(Fig. 2c–e) and the successful adaptive laboratory evolution (ALE)-mediated tolerance
of Au3+ toxicity imply the active involvement of membrane-associated reductase
enzymes during stepwise adaptation. These enzymes may function synergistically with
intracellular electron donors (e.g., NADH, glutathione) to nucleate and stabilize Au
NPs. We thank the reviewer again for highlighting this important mechanistic point.

acid, acetic acid, and pyruvic acid, which are typical intermediates of the mixed-acid
fermentation pathway employed by Actinobacillus succinogenes. The metabolic
network of A. succinogenes naturally branches between the C3 pathway (leading to
acetic/formic acid via pyruvate and acetyl-CoA) and the C4 reductive TCA pathway
(leading to succinate), which compete for common precursors and cofactors such as
NADH and PEP (phosphoenolpyruvate).
Importantly, our PEC-biohybrid system increased the succinic acid selectivity
from 44% (in native A. succinogenes) to 52% (with the NiO@PAA@NHS/Au@A.
succinogenes photoelectrode), as shown in Fig. R1-4.

This improvement is attributed to several synergistic factors: (1) Photogenerated

metabolic shift toward the C4 pathway; (3) The internal Au NPs facilitate enhanced
electron flux across the bacterial membrane, reducing redox bottlenecks and directing
metabolic flux toward succinate. Nonetheless, we fully acknowledge that achieving
selectivity >60% remains a challenge. In future work, product specificity can be
enhanced through metabolic engineering of A. succinogenes, photoelectrode and
electron supply optimization, and post-reaction purification and separation.

intracellular charge mediators.
Cytochrome bd oxidases (Cyt b I and Cyt b II are terminal oxidases that facilitate
electron transfer from the ubiquinol pool to molecular oxygen. These proteins are also
annotated in the A. succinogenes genome and classified under EC 7.1.1.7. Structurally,

We did not provide Faraday efficiency value in this work. The primary reason for not
providing Faradaic efficiency data is that, unlike traditional inorganic electrocatalytic
systems where electron transfer pathways and products are well-defined, the
photoelectrochemical-biohybrid system presents inherent complexities. In such hybrid
architectures, microorganisms not only serve as biocatalysts but also require energy
allocation for self-maintenance. Thousands of concurrent biochemical reactions
involving electron participation occur simultaneously, complicating the precise tracing
of electron flux. Furthermore, the energy supply in this system is not exclusively derived
from photoelectrode-generated electrons, which primarily function as auxiliary
contributors. A significant portion of metabolic energy originates from the organism's
internal ATP conversion processes. Consequently, the conventional concept of
Faradaic efficiency becomes less critical and less applicable in evaluating the
performance of biohybrid systems, as it fails to account for these multifaceted energy
transduction mechanisms and distributed electron utilization pathways.

We fully acknowledge that scaling up light-driven biohybrid systems for industrial
applications presents substantial challenges, particularly regarding light distribution,
reactor geometry, and energy efficiency. These are critical issues that must be addressed
before commercialization can be realized.
Recent advances, however, provide promising strategies to overcome these
limitations. For example, computational fluid dynamics (CFD)-optimized plate-type
airlift photobioreactors have demonstrated enhanced light utilization efficiency and
reduced energy consumption, offering viable design options for scalable
photobiocatalysis (Engineering 3, 318–329 (2017)). Furthermore, successful scale-up
examples in cyanobacterial systems have shown that closed photobioreactors (PBRs)
combined with continuous cultivation strategies can maintain high productivity with
sustainable energy inputs (Renew. Sustain. Energy Rev. 154, 111852 (2022)).
Key engineering considerations include achieving uniform illumination, optimized
mixing patterns, and high biomass retention. For instance, transparent grid-column
PBRs have been used to enable continuous hydrogen production with improved light
penetration, while Box-Behnken Design (BBD) optimized operational parameters have
been applied to maximize light absorption and biochemical productivity (Bioresour.

photobioreactors, which offer a high surface-area-to-volume ratio, outperform other
geometries for bacterial growth and hydrogen production (J. Clean. Prod. 181, 318–
328 (2018)).
Although significant challenges remain, these technological advances — including
real-time parameter control, modular reactor design, and optimized light distribution

provide a more balanced and realistic perspective on the opportunities and challenges

Faradaic Efficiency (FE)
While I understand the challenges in determining Faradaic efficiency, it remains a
critical metric in evaluating (photo)electrochemical systems, including biohybrids.
